# The Proofreader
## To the Eye of the Reader

**Since** it is a common saying in the mouths of our Sages that "he who gains honor through the disgrace of his fellow has no share in the World to Come," I have firmly resolved—heaven forbid—not to mention the names of the previous editions that appeared before us. In those places where I found "the word of the King and His law" <note>A biblical idiom from the Book of Esther, here referring to the sacred text of the Torah.</note>, whether in the letters, the vowels, or the cantillation marks, I found it overflowing with countless errors. This "portion worthy of honor" <note>original: "Ha-khitikhah ha-ra'uyah le-hitkabed" — a Talmudic expression for something of such high quality it can be served to distinguished guests.</note> shall testify for itself, and the eyes of all shall see clearly how it has been changed for the better compared to all that preceded it. For if my memory does not fail me <note>original: "ikhziv" — literally "to lie," a poetic way of saying his memory is reliable.</note>, I have corrected and proofread more than three hundred errors. And even though mistakes are inevitable due to human nature, and just as it is "impossible for grain to be without straw" <note>A common Rabbinic proverb meaning that no human work is perfect.</note>, so it is impossible for a printed work to be without errors; nevertheless, these will at least be greatly diminished. Perhaps those that remain will be few in number, for with all my strength and with vigorous love, I strove to examine it letter by letter, word by word—the script, the vowels, and the musical accents—to "show the peoples and the princes its beauty," for it is "fair to look upon" <note>quoting the Book of Esther (1:11) to describe the aesthetic and technical perfection of the printing.</note>. This shall be a memorial of merit for me wherever this book arrives. And "let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands" <note>Psalm 90:17</note>.

->Lover of the Sages<-

The humble <note>original: "Ha-Tza'ir" — literally "the young," a standard signature of humility used by Rabbis.</note> Menasseh ben Israel

<summary>In this preface, the renowned Amsterdam printer and Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel defends the necessity of his new edition, claiming to have corrected over 300 errors found in previous printings of the Hebrew Bible.</summary>
<keywords>Menasseh ben Israel, proofreading, printing history, Amsterdam, Hebrew grammar, typography, rabbinic idioms, biblical accents</keywords>

The Book of Genesis, Chapter 1

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative border composed of intricate floral and scrollwork patterns surrounds the central word "In the Beginning" <note>Hebrew: *Bereshit*</note>.</image-desc>

# Genesis

<insert>Chapter I</insert>
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. And the earth was <term>unformed and void</term> <note>Hebrew: *tohu va-vohu*; this phrase suggests a state of primordial chaos or emptiness before God began the work of ordering the world.</note>, and darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the surface of the waters. And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good; and God separated the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.

And God said, "Let there be an <term>expanse</term> <note>Hebrew: *rakia*; often translated as "firmament," it refers to the sky viewed as a physical dome that separates the waters above from the waters below.</note> in the midst of the waters, and let it separate between water and water." And God made the expanse, and He separated the water that was below the expanse from the water that was above the expanse; and it was so. And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, a second day.

And God said, "Let the waters below the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear"; and it was so. And God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters He called

<column-break/>

Seas; and God saw that it was good. And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation: seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees on the earth that yield fruit after their kind with its seed within it"; and it was so. And the earth brought forth vegetation: seed-bearing plants after their kind, and trees yielding fruit with its seed within it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, a third day.

And God said, "Let there be <term>luminaries</term> <note>Hebrew: *me'orot*; these are the celestial bodies, such as the sun and moon, which serve as "lamps" for the world.</note> in the expanse of the heaven to separate between the day and the night; and let them serve as signs and for appointed times, and for days and years. And let them be for luminaries in the expanse of the heaven to give light upon the earth"; and it was so. And God made the two great luminaries: the greater luminary to rule the day, and the lesser luminary to rule the night, and the stars. And God set them in the expanse of the heaven to give light upon the earth, and to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate between the light and between

1
I 2
<meta>catchword: and between</meta>

<meta>The previous page provided the opening verses of the Book of Genesis. # MENASSEH BEN ISRAEL
## To the Reader.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
I thought it worthwhile to briefly inform you of what I have achieved in this edition. I have applied the most diligent correction possible. I have faithfully amended all the errors—which were not few in previously published copies—pertaining to the <term>vowel points</term> <note>original: "punctis"; Hebrew is written primarily with consonants, and "points" or dots are added to indicate vowels and pronunciation.</note>, the letters, and even the rules of certain passages, after carefully noting them. Throughout this entire work, I have used four of the most accurate editions, and wherever a discrepancy appeared, I took refuge in grammatical rules and the <term>Masorah</term> <note>The Masorah is a traditional system of notes and rules intended to preserve the exact text and pronunciation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. My only aim was to follow truth in charity, without disparaging or diminishing the labor or work previously performed by anyone else. I am, of course, mindful of that Rabbinic saying: *“He who honors himself through the shame of his fellow has no portion in the world to come.”* <note>original: "Qui se onerat cum ignominia socij , non habet partem in futuro seculo." This is a Latin translation of a well-known Jewish ethical teaching.</note> I trust that this labor of mine will be pleasing to all the pious. Farewell and enjoy.

<meta>This page contains the Latin preface by the editor, Menasseh Ben Israel, detailing his editorial methodology. It precedes the biblical text of the Hebrew Bible. # MENASSEH BEN ISRAEL
## To the Reader.

I have thought it worthwhile to briefly inform you what has been achieved by me in this edition. I have applied the most diligent correction possible; errors both in the vowel points <note>The dots and marks used in Hebrew to indicate vowels, as the alphabet consists primarily of consonants.</note> and in the letters—and even in the very rules <note>Referring to the technical laws of Hebrew grammar and cantillation.</note> of certain passages, of which I found not a few in the editions published until now—I have faithfully amended them all after carefully noting them. Throughout this entire work, I have used four of the most accurate editions, and where any discrepancy arose, I sought recourse in grammatical rules and the Masorah <note>original: "Meffara" (an archaic printing of Massora); the traditional system of notes and rules used to ensure the accurate transmission of the Hebrew Bible text.</note>. My goal was none other than to follow the truth in charity, without casting blame or causing loss to the work and labor previously performed by anyone else. For I am well aware of that saying of the Rabbis <note>original: "Rabbinorum dicti."</note>: *He who honors himself through the shame of his fellow has no share in the world to come.* <note>A famous ethical teaching from the Talmud (Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1) warning against building one's reputation by belittling others.</note> I trust that this labor of mine will be pleasing to all the pious. Farewell and enjoy.

Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. # And He Heard

**Jethro**, the priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses, heard of **all** that God had done for Moses and for Israel His people—how the **LORD** had brought Israel out of Egypt. The name of the first was **Gershom** <note>original: *Gershom*, meaning "a stranger there"</note>, for he said, "I have been a stranger in a foreign land." And the name of the other was **Eliezer** <note>original: *Eliezer*, meaning "my God is help"</note>, for he said, "The God of my father was my help and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh."

And Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the **Mountain of God**. They asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent.

Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the **LORD** had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, and all the hardship <note>original: *tala'ah*, referring to the exhaustion and travail of the journey</note> they had encountered on the way, and how the **LORD** had delivered them. ### The Waters of Rephidim

And if a man strikes his servant or his maidservant with a rod and they die under his hand, they shall surely be avenged. But if they survive for a day or two, they shall not be avenged, for they are his property.
<note>While harsh to modern ears, this was a revolutionary restriction on a master's power, making them legally accountable for the death of a servant.</note>

<margin>36</margin> hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
<note>This principle, known as Lex Talionis ("Law of Retaliation"), was interpreted by ancient Jewish scholars as a requirement for monetary compensation of equal value, rather than literal physical mutilation.</note>

# Pekudei <note>original: "פקודי"; the name of this Torah portion, meaning "Accountings" or "Records"</note>

->Signature 40<-

Thus all the work of the **Tabernacle** <note>original: "Mishkan"; the portable dwelling place for the Divine Presence</note> of the Tent of Meeting was finished. The Israelites did according to all that the **Lord** <note>original: "YHWH"; the four-letter name of God, usually rendered as the LORD</note> had commanded Moses; so they did.

And they brought the Tabernacle to Moses: the tent and <margin>Missing <note>likely a scribal note regarding "defective" spelling or a missing letter in the manuscript tradition</note></margin> all its vessels, its hooks, its frames, its bars, its pillars, and its bases; the covering of tanned ram skins dyed red, the covering of **tahash** <note>original: "techashim"; an animal of uncertain identity, sometimes translated as "sea-cow," "dolphin," or "fine leather"</note> skins, and the screening veil; the Ark of the Testimony and its poles, and the mercy seat <note>original: "kapporet"; the golden lid of the Ark</note>; the table and all its vessels, and the **showbread** <note>original: "lechem hapanim"; literally "bread of the presence," twelve loaves displayed in the sanctuary</note>; the pure lampstand with its lamps—the lamps set in order—and all its vessels, and the oil for the light; the golden altar, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, and the screen for the entrance of the tent; the bronze altar and its bronze grating, its poles and all its vessels, the basin and its base; the hangings of the courtyard, its pillars and its bases, and the screen for the gate of the courtyard, its cords and its pegs; and all the tools for the service of the Tabernacle, for the Tent of Meeting; the woven garments for officiating in the sanctuary, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons to serve as priests.

According to all that the **Lord** had commanded Moses, so the Israelites did all the work. Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; just as the **Lord** had commanded, so they had done. And Moses blessed them.

<note>This "פ" represents a "Petuchah," a major paragraph break in the Hebrew text.</note>

And the **Lord** spoke to

<column-break/>

Moses, saying: On the first day of the first month <note>the month of Nisan, marking the start of the religious calendar in the spring</note>, on the first of the month, you shall set up the Tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting.

You shall put the Ark of the Testimony there, and you shall screen the Ark with the veil. You shall bring in the table and set its arrangement in order; you shall bring in the lampstand and light its lamps. You shall set the golden altar for incense before the Ark of the Testimony, and you shall put up the screen for the entrance to the Tabernacle.

You shall set the altar of burnt offering before the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting. You shall set the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and you shall put water there. You shall set up the courtyard all around, and put up the screen for the gate of the courtyard.

You shall take the anointing oil and anoint the Tabernacle and everything in it; you shall sanctify it and all its vessels, and it shall be holy. You shall anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its vessels, and sanctify the altar; the altar shall be **most holy** <note>original: "kodesh kodashim"; a status of supreme sanctity</note>. You shall anoint the basin and its base and sanctify it.

You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water. You shall clothe Aaron in the holy garments, and you shall anoint him and sanctify him, so that he may serve Me as a priest. You shall bring his sons and clothe them in tunics. You shall anoint them as you anointed their father, so they may serve Me as priests; and their anointing shall serve them for an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations.

### The Law of Offerings

פ <note>This Hebrew letter 'Pe' marks a 'Pethuchah,' a major paragraph break in the Torah scroll.</note>

The **Lord** spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering <term>Chattat</term> <note>original: "Chattat"; an offering brought for unintentional sins or ritual purification</note>: In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the sin offering shall be slaughtered before the **Lord**; it is most holy. The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Anything that touches its flesh shall become holy; and if any of its blood is spattered on a garment, <margin>The letter 'D' (Dalet)</margin> you shall wash that on which it was spattered in a holy place. A clay vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken; but if it is boiled in a copper vessel, it shall be scoured and rinsed with water. Every male among the priests may eat it; it is most holy. But no sin offering from which any of the blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place shall be eaten; it shall be burned with fire.

פ And this is the law of the guilt offering <term>Asham</term> <note>original: "Asham"; an offering brought for specific offenses such as misappropriating sacred property or breach of trust</note>: it is most holy. In the place where they slaughter the burnt offering, they shall slaughter the guilt offering, and its blood shall be dashed against the sides of the altar. All its fat shall be offered: the fat tail and the fat that covers the inner parts; the two kidneys and the fat that is on them at the loins; and the long lobe of the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys. The priest shall burn them on the altar as an offering by fire to the **Lord**; it is a guilt offering.

<column-break/>

Every male among the priests may eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place; it is most holy. The guilt offering is like the sin offering—there is one law for them: it shall belong to the priest who makes atonement with it. And the priest who offers anyone's burnt offering shall keep for himself the hide of the burnt offering he has offered. Also, every grain offering <term>Minchah</term> that is baked in an oven and all that is prepared in a pan or on a griddle shall belong to the priest who offers it. But every grain offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, shall belong to all the sons of Aaron, to one as much as the other.

ס <note>This Hebrew letter 'Samekh' marks a 'Setumah,' a minor paragraph break.</note>

And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings <term>Shelamim</term> <note>Sacrifices offered to celebrate fellowship or gratitude</note> which one may offer to the **Lord**: If he offers it for thanksgiving <term>Todah</term>, then he shall offer with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened cakes mixed with oil, unleavened wafers spread with oil, and cakes of fine flour well-mixed with oil. He shall bring his offering with cakes of leavened bread <term>Chametz</term> along with his sacrifice of thanksgiving peace offerings. From each kind of offering he shall present one cake as a gift <term>Terumah</term> <note>A contribution or "heave-offering" set aside for the priest</note> to the **Lord**; it shall belong to the priest who dashes the blood of the peace offerings. The flesh of the sacrifice of his thanksgiving peace offerings shall be eaten on the day it is offered; he shall not leave any of it until morning.

But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow <term>Neder</term> or a voluntary gift <term>Nedavah</term>, it shall be eaten on the day he offers his sacrifice, and on the next day what is left of it may be eaten. But what is left of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned with fire. If any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings is eaten on the third day, it shall not be accepted; it shall not be credited to the one who offers it. It shall be a rejected thing <term>Piggul</term> <note>original: "Piggul"; meat from a sacrifice that has become offensive or unfit because it was not eaten within the allotted time</note>; and the person who eats of it shall bear his iniquity.

You shall not go out from the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed; for it will take seven days to **ordain you** <note>original: "yemale et yedchem" — literally, "to fill your hands."</note>.
As has been done this day, so the **Lord** has commanded to be done to make atonement for you.
At the entrance of the Tent of Meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, keeping the **Lord’s** charge so that you do not die; for so I have been commanded."
And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the **Lord** commanded through Moses.

Often translated as leprosy, but in the Bible, it refers to a range of skin diseases, molds, or fungal growths that cause ritual impurity.</note>.

->MARK<-
<note>Hebrew: נֶגַע (Nega). This denotes a physical mark or plague-spot.</note>

When the mark of *Tzara'at* is on a person, then he shall be brought to the priest. And the priest shall look, and behold, if there is a white swelling on the skin, and it has turned the hair white, and there is a patch of living flesh <note>Hebrew: מִחְיַת בָּשָׂר חַי. This refers to raw or healthy-looking skin appearing within the white swelling.</note> in the swelling; it is a chronic *Tzara'at* in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean; he shall not shut him up <note>i.e., not isolate him for a trial period.</note>, for he is already unclean. 

And if the *Tzara'at* breaks out and spreads in the skin, and the *Tzara'at* covers all the skin of the afflicted person from his head to his feet, as far as the priest can see; then the priest shall look, and behold, if the *Tzara'at* has covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce the mark pure; it has all turned white, he is pure. 

But on the day that living flesh appears in him, he shall be unclean. And the priest shall see the living flesh and pronounce him unclean; the living flesh is unclean; it is *Tzara'at*. Or if the living flesh turns again and is changed to white, then he shall come to the priest. And the priest shall see him, and behold, if the mark is turned to white, then the priest shall pronounce the mark pure; he is pure.

And when there is flesh, and there was in its skin a boil <term>Sh'chin</term> <note>Hebrew: שְׁחִין. A shiny or glazy patch of skin.</note>, reddish-white, it shall be shown to the priest. And the priest shall look, and behold, if its appearance is lower than the skin and its hair has turned white, the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is the mark of *Tzara'at* broken out in the boil.

# After the Death
<note>Hebrew: "Acharei Mot," the title of this Torah portion, referring to the death of Aaron's sons mentioned at the start of chapter 16.</note>

...[any man] who slaughters an ox, or a lamb, or a goat within the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp; and has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to present it as an offering to the **LORD** before the Tabernacle of the **LORD**, bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man—he has shed blood—and that man shall be cut off <term>cut off: "Karet," a spiritual penalty involving excision from the community and the divine presence</term> from among his people. This is so that the children of Israel may bring their sacrifices, which they currently sacrifice in the open field, and bring them to the **LORD** at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, to the priest, and sacrifice them as peace offerings <term>peace offerings: "Shelamim," sacrifices intended to express well-being and shared as a meal between the donor, the priest, and the altar</term> to the **LORD**. And the priest shall splash the blood against the altar of the **LORD** at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, and turn the fat into smoke as a pleasing aroma to the **LORD**. And they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the goat-demons <note>original: "Se'irim," likely referring to wilderness spirits or idols shaped like goats</note> after whom they stray. This shall be a lasting statute for them throughout their generations. And you shall say to them: Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who reside among them, who offers up a burnt offering or a sacrifice, and does not bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to offer it to the **LORD**, that man shall be cut off from his people. And any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who reside among them, who consumes any blood, I will set My face against that person who consumes the blood, and I will cut them off from among their people. For the life <note>original: "Nefesh," meaning soul or life-force</note> of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your lives; for it is the blood that makes atonement by means of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel: No person among you shall consume blood, nor shall the stranger who resides among you consume

<column-break/>

blood. And any man of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who reside among them, who hunts and catches any beast or bird that may be eaten, he shall pour out its blood and cover it with dust. For the life of all flesh—its blood is its life; and I said to the children of Israel: You shall not consume the blood of any flesh, for the life of all flesh is its blood; anyone who consumes it shall be cut off. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: If a man or a woman makes a special vow, a <term>Nazirite</term> <note>original: "Nazir" - one who is consecrated or set apart</note> vow, to set themselves apart for the LORD; he shall abstain from wine and strong drink. He shall not drink wine vinegar or strong drink vinegar, nor shall he drink any grape juice, nor shall he eat grapes, whether fresh or dried. All the days of his consecration, he shall eat nothing that is produced from the grapevine, from the seeds even to the skins. 

All the days of his Nazirite vow, no razor shall pass over his head. Until the days that he has set himself apart for the LORD are completed, he shall be holy; he shall let the hair of his head grow long. All the days of his consecration to the LORD, he shall not go near a dead person. Even for his father, his mother, his brother, or his sister, he shall not make himself <term>unclean</term> <note>ritual impurity (tum'ah) prevents a person from participating in sacred activities</note> when they die, for the crown of his God is upon his head. All the days of his consecration he is holy to the LORD.

And if someone dies very suddenly near him, thereby defiling his consecrated head, he shall shave his head on the day of his purification; on the seventh day he shall shave it. On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The priest shall offer one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him because he sinned by reason of the dead body; and he shall sanctify his head on that same day. He shall reconsecrate to the LORD the days of his vow and bring a yearling lamb for a guilt offering; the previous days shall be void, because his consecration was defiled.

And this is the law of the Nazirite: on the day his days of consecration are fulfilled, he shall be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. And he shall bring his offering to the LORD...

...one yearling lamb without blemish for a burnt offering, one yearling ewe lamb without blemish for a sin offering, and one ram without blemish for a peace offering; and a basket of unleavened bread, cakes of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil, along with their grain offerings and their drink offerings. The priest shall bring them before the LORD and perform the service for his sin offering and his burnt offering. He shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread; the priest shall also offer its grain offering and its drink offering. 

Then the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting; he shall take the hair of his consecrated head and put it on the fire which is under the sacrifice of the peace offerings. The priest shall take the cooked shoulder of the ram, one unleavened cake from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the palms of the Nazirite after he has shaved his consecrated hair. The priest shall wave them as a wave offering before the LORD; it is a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution. After that, the Nazirite may drink wine. 

This is the law of the Nazirite who makes a vow—his offering to the LORD for his consecration, in addition to whatever else his hand can afford. ...to them: If any man’s wife goes astray and behaves unfaithfully toward him, and another man has had sexual relations with her, but it is hidden from the eyes of her husband and she remains undiscovered; if she has defiled herself and there is no witness against her, and she was not caught in the act; and if a spirit of jealousy comes upon him and he is jealous of his wife and she has defiled herself—or if a spirit of jealousy comes upon him and he is jealous of his wife and she has not defiled herself—then the man shall bring his wife to the priest. He shall bring the offering required for her, one-tenth of an <term>ephah</term> <note>about 2 liters or 2.2 quarts</note> of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a <term>grain offering of jealousy</term>, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to mind.

The priest shall bring her forward and have her stand before the LORD. The priest shall take holy water in an earthen vessel; and the priest shall take some of the dust that is on the floor of the <term>Tabernacle</term> <note>the portable dwelling place of God's presence</note> and put it into the water. The priest shall have the woman stand before the LORD, and shall loosen the hair of the woman’s head <note>original: "u-fara," which can mean uncovering the head or unbinding the hair as a sign of mourning or public shame</note>, and put the grain offering of remembrance in her hands, which is the grain offering of jealousy. In the priest’s hand shall be the bitter water that brings a curse. Then the priest shall put her under oath and say to the woman, “If no man has lain with you, and if you have not gone astray into <term>impurity</term> <note>ritual or moral defilement</note> while under your husband’s authority, be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse. But if you have gone astray while under your husband’s authority, and if you have defiled yourself and some man other than your husband has had sexual relations with you”—then the priest shall put the woman under the oath of the curse, and the priest shall say to the woman—“the LORD make you

<column-break/>

a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your belly swell. May this water that brings a curse enter your stomach and make your belly swell and your thigh fall away.” And the woman shall say, “<term>Amen, Amen</term>” <note>a Hebrew word meaning "So be it" or "it is true," spoken twice here to confirm the acceptance of the oath</note>.

Then the priest shall write these curses in a scroll and wash them off into the bitter water. He shall make the woman drink the bitter water that brings a curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain. The priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy from the woman’s hand, and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar. The priest shall take a handful of the grain offering as its memorial portion and turn it into smoke on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water. When he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has been unfaithful to her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people. But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be immune and be able to conceive children.

This is the law of jealousies, when a wife goes astray while under her husband’s authority and defiles herself, or when a spirit of jealousy comes upon a man and he is jealous of his wife; then he shall have the woman stand before the LORD, and the priest shall apply this entire law to her. The man shall be free from <term>iniquity</term> <note>guilt or punishment</note>, but that woman shall bear her iniquity.

So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites. Two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon, according to their service. And four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari, according to their service, under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest. But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because the service of the holy objects was upon them; they had to carry them on their shoulders.
The leaders then presented the dedication offering for the altar on the day it was anointed; the leaders presented their offerings before the altar. And the Lord said to Moses: "One leader each day, one leader each day, shall they present their offering for the dedication of the altar."

**This is the law:** When a man dies in a tent: everyone who comes into the tent and everything that is in the tent shall be unclean for seven days. And every open vessel that does not have a seal <note>original: 'tzamid patil' — a cover fastened with a cord</note> fastened upon it is unclean. And whoever touches one in the open field who has been slain by the sword, or a corpse, or a human bone, or a grave, shall be unclean for seven days. 

And for the unclean person, they shall take some of the ashes of the burnt **purification offering** <term>chattat: usually 'sin offering,' but here specifically referring to the Red Heifer ashes</term> and put **living water** <note>original: 'mayim chayim' — fresh, running spring water as opposed to stagnant water</note> on it in a vessel. And a clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it upon the tent, upon all the vessels, and upon the persons who were there, and upon the one who touched the bone, or the slain, or the corpse, or the grave. 

And the clean person shall sprinkle upon the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day; and on the seventh day he shall purify him <note>or 'absolve him from sin'</note>, and he shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and he shall be clean in the evening. But the man who is unclean and does not purify himself, that soul shall be cut off from the midst of the congregation, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the **LORD**; the water of lustration was not sprinkled upon him—he is unclean. 

And it shall be a perpetual statute for them: the one who sprinkles the water of lustration shall wash his clothes, and the one who touches the water of lustration shall be unclean until evening. And whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean, and the person who touches it shall be unclean until evening.

<summary>King Balak of Moab repeatedly attempts to use the prophet Balaam to curse the Israelites from different vantage points, but each time Balaam is divinely compelled to bless them instead. These oracles emphasize Israel's unique destiny, their vast numbers, and the immutability of God's blessing over them.</summary>

Every vow and every binding oath to afflict the soul, her husband may uphold it or her husband may annul it. But if her husband remains silent toward her from day to day, then he upholds all her vows or all her bonds which are upon her; he has upheld them because he remained silent toward her on the day he heard them. But if he truly annuls them after he has heard them, then he shall bear her iniquity. These are the statutes which the Lord commanded Moses, between a man and his wife.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Execute the vengeance of the children of Israel on the Midianites; afterward you shall be gathered to your people.” <note>The phrase "gathered to your people" is a biblical expression for death, indicating this was to be Moses's final major act of leadership.</note> And Moses spoke to the people, saying, “Arm men from among you for the army, and let them go against Midian to execute the Lord’s vengeance on Midian. Also purify every garment, everything made of leather, everything woven of goats’ hair, and everything made of wood.”

Then Eleazar the priest said to the men of the army who had gone to the battle, “This is the <term>statute of the law</term><note>original: "chukat ha-Torah"—a term denoting a foundational divine decree.</note> which the Lord commanded Moses: Only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead—everything that can endure fire—you shall put through the fire, and it shall be clean; nevertheless it must be purified with the <term>water of cleansing</term><note>original: "mei niddah"—ritually prepared water used to remove the impurity of death.</note>; and all that cannot endure fire you shall put through water. And you shall wash your clothes on the seventh day and be clean, and afterward you may come into the camp.”

# Book of Numbers

->### The Journeys of Israel<-
<meta>catchword: And they journeyed</meta>

They journeyed from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the day after the Passover sacrifice, the children of Israel went out with a high hand <note>original: "be-yad ramah" – meaning they left triumphantly and publicly, not as fleeing slaves.</note> in the sight of all the Egyptians. 

And the Egyptians were burying those whom the LORD had struck among them, every firstborn; and upon their gods the LORD executed judgments <note>This refers to the spiritual and physical defeat of Egypt's deities during the Ten Plagues.</note>.

The children of Israel journeyed from Rameses and camped in Succoth.

They journeyed from Succoth and camped in Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness.

They journeyed from Etham and turned back toward Pi-hahiroth, which is before Baal-zephon, and they camped before Migdol.

They journeyed from before Pi-hahiroth and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness; they went a three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham and camped in Marah <note>Literally "bitter," named for the bitter waters found there.</note>.

They journeyed from Marah and came to Elim; and in Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy date palms, and they camped there.

They journeyed from Elim and camped by the Sea of Reeds <note>traditionally the Red Sea</note>.

They journeyed from the Sea of Reeds and camped in the Wilderness of Sin.

They journeyed from the Wilderness of Sin and camped in Dophkah.

They journeyed from Dophkah and camped in Alush.

They journeyed from Alush and camped in Rephidim, and there was no water there for the people to drink.

They journeyed from Rephidim and camped in the Wilderness of Sinai.

They journeyed from the Wilderness of Sinai and camped in Kibroth Hattaavah <note>Literally "the Graves of Craving."</note>.

They journeyed from Kibroth Hattaavah and camped in Hazeroth.

They journeyed from Hazeroth and camped in Rithmah.

They journeyed from Rithmah and camped in Rimmon-perez.

They journeyed from Rimmon-perez and camped in Libnah.

They journeyed from Libnah and camped in Rissah.

<column-break/>

They journeyed from Rissah and camped in Kehelathah.

They journeyed from Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher.

They journeyed from Mount Shepher and camped in Haradah.

They journeyed from Haradah and camped in Makheloth.

They journeyed from Makheloth and camped in Tahath.

The blood redeemer <note>original: "goel ha-dam" – the next of kin who had the legal right and duty to avenge a relative's death.</note> himself shall put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death. And if he pushed him out of hatred, or hurled something at him by lying in wait <note>original: "bi-tzediyah" – with malicious intent or ambush.</note> so that he died; or in enmity he struck him with his hand so that he died, the one who struck him shall surely be put to death, for he is a murderer. But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled any object at him without lying in wait, or with any stone by which one may die, without seeing him, and it fell upon him and he died, while he was not his enemy <margin>2</margin> and did not seek his harm: then the assembly shall judge between the striker and the blood redeemer according to these laws. shall tread upon their high places. -> <note>original: ס (Setumah) — A "closed" paragraph break in the Torah scroll, indicating a thematic pause.</note> <-
Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount
Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho.
And the **LORD** showed him all the land:
Gilead as far as Dan; all of Naphtali,
the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the
land of Judah as far as the Western Sea; the
Negev, and the Plain—the Valley of Jericho, the City
of Palms—as far as Zoar. And the **LORD** said
to him, "This is the land of which I swore
to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying,
'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes,
but you shall not cross over there." So Moses, the
servant of the **LORD**, died there in the land of Moab, according to the
word of the **LORD**. And He buried him in the valley, in the land of
Moab, opposite Beth-peor; but no man knows
his burial place to this day.
Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died;
his eye was not dim, nor his vigor abated.
And the children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of
Moab for thirty days; then the days of weeping
and mourning for Moses ended. And Joshua son of Nun was full of
the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands
upon him; so the children of Israel listened to him and did
as the **LORD** had commanded Moses.
But there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses,
whom the **LORD** knew face to face.
For all

...the ancient hills. And with the best things of the earth and its fullness,
and the favor of Him who dwelt in the bush <note>A reference to God's appearance to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3.</note>. Let these blessings come upon the head of
Joseph, and upon the crown of the head of the prince of his brothers. His firstborn
ox is his majesty, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox <note>original: רְאֵם (Re'em) — Traditionally translated as 'unicorn' or 'wild ox', signifying immense strength.</note>; with them
he shall gore the nations, all together, to the ends of the earth; and they are
the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.

And of Zebulun he said: Rejoice,
Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents.
They shall call peoples to the mountain; there they shall offer sacrifices of
righteousness; for they shall suck the abundance of the seas and the hidden
treasures of the sand.
-> <note>original: ס (Setumah) — A "closed" paragraph break.</note> <-
And of Gad he said: Blessed is He who enlarges Gad! Like a lion
he dwells, and tears the arm and even the crown of the head. He chose the
best part for himself, for there the portion of the lawgiver <note>Moses is often identified as the "lawgiver" (Mechoqeq) who was buried in the territory of Gad.</note>
was hidden; and he came with the heads of the people; the righteousness of the **LORD**
he executed, and His judgments with Israel.
-> <note>original: ס (Setumah) — A "closed" paragraph break.</note> <-
And of Dan he said: Dan is a lion's
cub that leaps forth from Bashan.
-> <note>original: ס (Setumah) — A "closed" paragraph break.</note> <-
And of Naphtali he said: O Naphtali, satisfied with favor
and full of the blessing of the **LORD**, possess the sea and the south.
-> <note>original: ס (Setumah) — A "closed" paragraph break.</note> <-
And of Asher he said:
Most blessed of sons be Asher; let him be favored by his brothers,
and let him dip his foot in oil. Your sandals shall be iron and bronze,
and as your days, so shall your strength be. There is none like God,
O Jeshurun <note>Jeshurun: A poetic and honorary name for the people of Israel, meaning "the upright ones."</note>, who rides the heavens to your help, and in His majesty
through the skies. The eternal God is a dwelling place, and underneath
are the everlasting arms; and He drove out the enemy from before you,
and said, "Destroy!" So Israel dwelt
in safety, the fountain of Jacob alone, in a land of grain
and wine; His heavens also drop down dew.

<summary>This page contains the final tribal blessings and the narrative of Moses' death on Mount Nebo. It emphasizes Moses' unique prophetic status and the transition of authority to Joshua as Israel prepares to enter the Promised Land.</summary>
